concept.name: Floyd-Warshall All-Pairs Shortest Paths

relationships.description: Connects Floyd-Warshall All-Pairs Shortest Paths to core algorithm patterns in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: A dynamic-programming algorithm that computes shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in O(V^3) time and O(V^2) space, handling negative edge weights and detecting negative cycles.
spark.keyTakeaway: With just three nested loops (`k` outermost), Floyd-Warshall solves all-pairs shortest paths and negative-cycle detection on dense graphs up to V ≈ 500 in milliseconds.

concept.whyItMatters: While Dijkstra finds shortest paths from one source on non-negative graphs, real systems often need an all-to-all distance matrix—such as intra-datacenter mesh latency tables, currency-arbitrage cross-rate graphs (which contain negative log-weights), or compiler call-graph transitive closures. Floyd-Warshall provides a compact, branch-predictable O(V^3) solution with zero priority-queue overhead.
whenToUse: Your graph is small to medium (`V <= 500`) and dense (`E ≈ V^2`), where O(V^3) tight loops beat V runs of Dijkstra in both constant factors and code simplicity.
Edge weights can be negative (e.g., `-log(exchange_rate)` in FX arbitrage or cost/rebate graphs) and you need to detect negative-weight cycles (`dist[i][i] < 0`).
You only need unweighted reachability (transitive closure), where Warshall's bitset variant runs in `O(V^3 / 64)` using bitwise `OR` instructions.
whenNotToUse: `V > 1,000` on a sparse graph (`E = O(V)`)—running Dijkstra V times (`O(V E log V)`) or Johnson's algorithm (`O(V^2 log V + V E)`) is 100x–1,000x faster.
You only need shortest paths from 1 or a few source nodes, where single-source Bellman-Ford (`O(V E)`) or Dijkstra (`O(E log V)`) avoids wasted all-pairs work.
Edges mutate frequently at runtime and `V > 200`; recomputing O(V^3) on every topology change stalls latency-sensitive routing.
keyPoints: The recurrence `dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j])` defines the shortest path from `i` to `j` using only intermediate vertices from `{0, ..., k}`.
The intermediate vertex loop `k` MUST be the outermost loop; placing `i` or `j` outside `k` breaks the DP invariant and misses multi-hop paths.

Because iteration `k` never modifies row `k` or column `k` in a way that affects `dist[i][k]` or `dist[k][j]` (assuming no negative self-loops), the 3D DP table collapses to a single `V x V` matrix updated in-place.
Negative-weight cycles exist if and only if any diagonal entry `dist[i][i] < 0` after the `k` loop finishes.
Path reconstruction requires a parallel `next[i][j]` matrix initialized to `j` for direct edges `(i, j)`, updated to `next[i][k]` whenever `dist[i][k] + dist[k][j] < dist[i][j]`.

examples.title: SDN / Multi-Region PoP Latency Matrix
examples.scenario: A cloud backbone controller manages `V = 180` Points of Presence (PoPs) in a near-complete mesh and computes optimal backup routing tables whenever link RTTs shift.
examples.outcome: `180^3 = 5.83 million` compare-and-add operations run in <4 ms in C++/Java over a contiguous 256 KB `int64` matrix (fitting in L2 cache), producing the full `180 x 180` routing matrix and `nextHop[i][j]` table.

examples.title: FX Currency Arbitrage Cycle Detection
examples.scenario: A trading engine monitors `V = 45` currencies with bid/ask conversion rates `r(i, j)`. By setting edge weights to `-ln(r(i, j))`, a profitable arbitrage loop corresponds to a cycle whose edge sum is `< 0`.
examples.outcome: Running Floyd-Warshall (`45^3 = 91,125` ops, <100 µs) immediately flags arbitrage opportunities whenever `dist[c][c] < -1e-9` and reconstructs the exact currency cycle via `next[c][c]`.

tradeOffs.pro: Three nested `for` loops over a flat `V x V` array auto-vectorize well and need no heap or adjacency list.
tradeOffs.con: Cubic `O(V^3)` growth hits a hard wall: `V = 2,000` requires `8 * 10^9` operations (several seconds to minutes).

tradeOffs.pro: Natively supports negative edge weights and negative-cycle detection without Johnson's reweighting step.
tradeOffs.con: Does redundant work if the graph is sparse (`E << V^2`) and weights are non-negative.

tradeOffs.pro: Updating `dist` in-place halves memory bandwidth and fits `V <= 512` matrices inside L2/L3 CPU cache.
tradeOffs.con: Cannot serve concurrent lock-free queries while `k` iterations are mid-flight without double-buffering.

failureModes.name: Wrong Loop Order (`i-j-k` Instead of `k-i-j`)
failureModes.description: Putting `i` and `j` as outer loops and `k` innermost evaluates `dist[i][k]` and `dist[k][j]` before higher-index intermediate paths are finalized, silently returning suboptimal distances.
failureModes.mitigation: Always structure loops strictly as `for k in 0..V: for i in 0..V: for j in 0..V` and verify against multi-hop test cases (e.g., 4-node chain).

failureModes.name: `INF + INF` Signed Integer Overflow
failureModes.description: Initializing unreachable pairs to `INT_MAX` (`2,147,483,647`) causes `dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]` to wrap around to negative numbers, corrupting the `min()` comparison.
failureModes.mitigation: Guard the inner step with `if (dist[i][k] == INF || dist[k][j] == INF) continue;` or use `INF = 1e15` inside `int64`.

failureModes.name: Unbounded Negative Cycle Cascading
failureModes.description: When a negative cycle exists, repeated relaxations drive `dist[i][j]` toward `-INF` and can overflow 64-bit integers if edges are large.
failureModes.mitigation: Clamp `dist[i][j]` at `-INF` or inspect `dist[k][k] < 0` immediately to abort and report the negative cycle.

failureModes.name: Stale `next[i][j]` Matrix on Tie-Breaking
failureModes.description: Updating `next[i][j] = next[i][k]` when `dist[i][k] + dist[k][j] == dist[i][j]` (non-strict inequality) can create self-referential loops in the `next` table when zero-weight cycles exist.
failureModes.mitigation: Update `next[i][j]` strictly on `<` (`if cand < dist[i][j]`), and keep `next[i][i] = i`.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to initialize the diagonal `dist[i][i] = 0` before running the `k` loop.
Overwriting parallel edges in a multigraph with the last edge instead of taking `min(dist[u][v], w)` during initialization.
Using `dist[i][j] = min(...)` with `INT_MAX` without checking for `INF` operands first.
Assuming `V = 3,000` is fast because `O(V^3)` looks simple—`2.7 * 10^10` iterations will time out.
Forgetting that `next[i][k]` (not `k`) must be stored in `next[i][j]` when relaxing via intermediate `k`.

sections.content:
## The idea

Floyd-Warshall builds shortest paths incrementally by restricting which **intermediate vertices** are allowed. Let `dp(k, i, j)` be the shortest path from `i` to `j` whose intermediate vertices (excluding `i` and `j`) all belong to `{0, 1, ..., k}`.

At step `k`, any optimal path from `i` to `j` either does not pass through vertex `k` (cost `dp(k-1, i, j)`) or splits at `k` into two subpaths that only use `{0, ..., k-1}` (cost `dp(k-1, i, k) + dp(k-1, k, j)`). Taking the minimum across all `(i, j)` for each `k` from `0` to `V - 1` solves all pairs in `O(V^3)` time.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider a 4-node directed graph (`0, 1, 2, 3`) with edges `0->1 (3)`, `1->2 (2)`, `2->3 (1)`, `0->3 (10)`, and `3->1 (-4)`:

1. **Init**: `dist[i][i] = 0`, `dist[0][3] = 10`, others per edges or `INF`.
2. **`k = 0`**: No incoming edges to `0`, matrix unchanged.
3. **`k = 1`**: Paths through `1`: `0->1->2` updates `dist[0][2] = 3 + 2 = 5`. `3->1->2` updates `dist[3][2] = -4 + 2 = -2`.
4. **`k = 2`**: Paths through `2`: `0->2->3` updates `dist[0][3] = min(10, 5 + 1) = 6`. `1->2->3` updates `dist[1][3] = 2 + 1 = 3`. Notice `3->2->3` gives `dist[3][3] = min(0, -2 + 1) = -1 < 0`!
5. **Cycle detected**: Because `dist[3][3] < 0` (`3 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3` has weight `-4 + 2 + 1 = -1`), Floyd-Warshall flags a negative cycle.

sections.content:
## Transitive closure and SIMD optimization

When edge weights are unweighted booleans (reachability only), **Warshall's algorithm** replaces `min` and `+` with bitwise `OR` and `AND`: `reach[i][j] |= reach[i][k] & reach[k][j]`. By packing each row `reach[i]` into `ceil(V / 64)` 64-bit words (or AVX2 256-bit vectors), the inner `j` loop collapses into `if (reach[i][k]) row_i |= row_k`.

This cuts runtime by 64x–256x, allowing `V = 2,000` transitive closure in ~15 ms. Even for weighted Floyd-Warshall, hoisting `if (dist[i][k] == INF) continue;` outside the inner `j` loop skips entire rows of `V` iterations on sparse graphs and lets compilers auto-vectorize the `j` loop with `vpaddq`/`vpminsq`.

## All-pairs shortest path algorithm comparison

| Algorithm | Time Complexity | Space | Negative Weights | Best Regime |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Floyd-Warshall** | `O(V^3)` | `O(V^2)` | Yes (detects neg cycles) | Dense graphs, `V <= 500`, FX arbitrage |
| **V x Dijkstra (Binary Heap)** | `O(V E log V)` | `O(V + E)` + output | No | Sparse graphs (`E = O(V)`), `V > 500` |
| **Johnson's Algorithm** | `O(V^2 log V + V E)` | `O(V^2)` | Yes (via Bellman-Ford) | Sparse graphs with negative edges |
| **Warshall Bitset** | `O(V^3 / 64)` | `O(V^2 / 8)` bytes | N/A (boolean) | Reachability / call-graph closure |

## Failure modes

- **Loop inversion (`i, j, k`)**: Running `k` as the innermost loop breaks optimal substructure and leaves multi-hop paths undiscovered.
- **Integer overflow**: Adding `INF + INF` or `INF + negative_edge` when `INF = INT_MAX` wraps to negative values; always guard `dist[i][k] != INF` and `dist[k][j] != INF`.
- **Negative cycle propagation**: If a node `u` can reach a negative cycle and reach `v`, `dist[u][v]` can underflow unless clamped or flagged via `dist[k][k] < 0`.
- **Path reconstruction infinite loop**: Updating `next[i][j]` on `<=` instead of `<` or failing to stop when `dist[i][i] < 0` causes `while (curr != end)` path reconstruction to spin forever.

## Incremental updates and real-world routing

When a single edge `(u, v)` decreases in weight, you do not always need a full `O(V^3)` rerun: checking `min(dist[i][j], dist[i][u] + new_w + dist[v][j])` for all `(i, j)` updates the entire matrix in `O(V^2)`. However, if an edge weight *increases* or an edge is deleted, paths that relied on `(u, v)` are invalidated, and you must recompute (or fall back to dynamic APSP algorithms).

In production network controllers (like SDN TE or inter-DC traffic matrices), Floyd-Warshall is typically capped at region/cluster-level aggregations (`V <= 300`), while host-level routing delegates to hierarchical Dijkstra or link-state OSPF.

## Practical checklist

- Confirm `V <= 500` (or `<= 2,000` for bitset transitive closure) before committing to `O(V^3)`.
- Place `k` strictly as the outermost loop, `i` second, `j` innermost for row-major cache locality.
- Guard both `dist[i][k] == INF` and `dist[k][j] == INF` before adding.
- Scan `dist[i][i] < 0` for all `i` after completion to detect negative cycles before trusting any distance.
- Hoist `dist[i][k]` into a local register outside the `j` loop to help the compiler auto-vectorize.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Floyd Warshall All Pairs

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: A dynamic-programming algorithm that computes shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in O(V^3) time and O(V^2) space, handling negative edge weights and detecting negative cycles.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Triple-Loop Relaxer applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Diagonal & Next-Hop.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Diagonal & Next-Hop experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Always structure loops strictly as `for k in 0..V: for i in 0..V: for j in 0..V` and verify against multi-hop test cases (e.g., 4-node chain).

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: With just three nested loops (`k` outermost), Floyd-Warshall solves all-pairs shortest paths and negative-cycle detection on dense graphs up to V ≈ 500 in milliseconds.
Avoid trap: Forgetting to initialize the diagonal `dist[i][i] = 0` before running the `k` loop.
Avoid trap: Overwriting parallel edges in a multigraph with the last edge instead of taking `min(dist[u][v], w)` during initialization.
When to reach for it: Your graph is small to medium (`V <= 500`) and dense (`E ≈ V^2`), where O(V^3) tight loops beat V runs of Dijkstra in both constant factors and code simplicity.
When to reach for it: Edge weights can be negative (e.g., `-log(exchange_rate)` in FX arbitrage or cost/rebate graphs) and you need to detect negative-weight cycles (`dist[i][i] < 0`).

putItTogether.title: Putting Floyd Warshall All Pairs Together
putItTogether.summary: With just three nested loops (`k` outermost), Floyd-Warshall solves all-pairs shortest paths and negative-cycle detection on dense graphs up to V ≈ 500 in milliseconds.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Floyd Warshall All Pairs before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: `180^3 = 5.83 million` compare-and-add operations run in <4 ms in C++/Java over a contiguous 256 KB `int64` matrix (fitting in L2 cache), producing the full `180 x 180` routing matrix and `nextHop[i][j]` table.
